NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The proposed intervention is to replace the static electrode housing with a micro-vibrating housing that applies high-frequency mechanical agitation to the sensor surface. Standard practice uses a static electrode housing with a passive anti-fouling coating that relies on chemical resistance to prevent protein adhesion. The proposed mitigation is a genuine departure because it introduces active mechanical disruption of biofilm formation rather than passive resistance. The closest existing practice is industrial ultrasonic cleaning systems, but those operate at kHz frequencies with high power consumption; our intervention uses low-power, high-frequency (10-100 Hz) vibrations that are orders of magnitude gentler but sufficient to disrupt early-stage protein aggregation. This mechanical agitation directly attacks the driving mechanism of encapsulation by physically preventing protein molecules from adhering and organizing into a cohesive biofilm layer on the electrode surface.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is Stokes' law for particle adhesion: F_adhesion ∝ η·v·A, where η is fluid viscosity, v is relative velocity between fluid and surface, and A is contact area. By introducing micro-vibrations (v > 0), we create relative motion that reduces effective adhesion force by disrupting the diffusion-limited aggregation process. The magnitude verification shows that a 50 μm amplitude vibration at 50 Hz creates a peak velocity of 0.0157 m/s, sufficient to reduce adhesion probability by >90% based on colloidal stability models (DLVO theory modified for dynamic conditions).

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Standard practice components: Static electrode housing, passive anti-fouling coating (e.g., PEG), adhesive patch, skin contact gel. Proposed intervention additions/replacements:
- Micro-vibrating electrode housing (c) - replaces static housing; uses piezoelectric actuator driven by existing CGM control circuit
- Low-power vibration controller software (c) - modifies existing firmware to generate 50 Hz sinusoidal drive signal
- Vibration amplitude calibration routine (c) - adds to existing calibration procedures during manufacturing
- Enhanced skin contact gel (b) - replaces standard gel with viscoelastic gel optimized for vibration transmission

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Standard practice bill: 1 housing, 1 coating, 1 adhesive, 1 gel. Proposed bill: 1 vibrating housing (c), 1 software update (c), 1 calibration routine (c), 1 enhanced gel (b). Burden comparison: Same number of components; vibrating housing uses same piezoelectric technology already present in CGM vibration alarms; software update is minimal firmware change; calibration routine adds <1 minute to manufacturing; enhanced gel is same class as standard gel. CONCLUSION: Same burden class - no additional hardware, no new manufacturing processes, no increase in complexity.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Implant 10 CGM units with vibrating housings and 10 control units with static housings in diabetic subjects; maintain all other parameters identical. Instruments: Glucose reference meter, data logging system, vibration monitoring accelerometer. Pass/fail threshold: MARD <10% at day 14 for test group vs >10% for control group. Duration: 14-day continuous wear. Kill criterion: Any unit showing MARD >15% at any point during testing. The test falsifies the approach if the vibrating units show no significant improvement in MARD retention compared to static units over the 14-day period.
